fixed.before: The law-giving hero happened to be carrying a rod in his hand; leaning on this staff while his right hand guided his step, he flung it down, cast out before him with a strong throw. Then — wonderful to tell — the wood stirred and began to creep: not as it puts forth from the shoot branches without sense, [...] moving only those which the fruits make grow, but creeping in a coil, and, by the use of a changed body, bearing sense and soul, the rod began to run along, and soon, reshaped, it presents a snake. Terrified, he stood fixed, and the tyrant, black for eternity, then turned pale in the face. But lest his attendant, standing by with wavering look, should see him confounded and yielding to such a sign, he conceals that he believes the thing was done by the highest command, wishing the deeds to be thought not divine but [mere illusions]. Then he orders whatever magicians, or men learned in spells, attempt with dire frauds the unlawful art of Egypt, to bring forth long staffs, compelling that his minister perform with funereal murmur the things that had been shown. Then, as ordered, they run together from all sides, and each arms his enchanted staff with the familiar charm; thrown down, they give empty appearances, and the supposed snakes frighten deluded eyes with a deceiving shape. Nor did the magicians swell [with pride] for long: all that they thought they had made is consumed; for the first horned snake, still biting, swallowed in its mouth the serpents feigned by art. After Moses closed the display of power, and, holding the victor by the tail, lifted it from the ground, the serpent gives way to wood, its face withdraws, and the wandering coils stiffened as the body hardened. Why say more? It becomes the former rod, with which the priest afterwards showed very many signs in the time that followed.

fixed.before: 23. A man once came to Scetis to become a monk. He also brought his son, newly weaned. When the son had become a young man, demons began to attack and tempt him. And he said to his father: I am going back to the world, because I cannot endure the desires of the flesh. His father comforted him. Then the young man said: I can no longer endure it, father; let me go back to the world. His father said to him: Listen to me, son, once more: take forty loaves and palm leaves for forty days, and go into the inner desert, and stay there forty days, and the will of God will be done. Obeying his father, he got up and went into the desert, and stayed there, working and making plaits of dry palm and eating dry bread. And when he had stayed there quietly for twenty days, behold, he saw a work of the devil coming upon him; and there stood before him what seemed an Ethiopian woman, stinking and foul to look at, so that he could not bear her stench, and he thrust her away from him. And she said to him: I am she who appears sweet in the hearts of men; but because of your obedience and the labour you endure, God has not permitted me to seduce you, but I have made my stench known to you. He got up and, giving thanks to God, came to his father and said to him: I no longer want to go to the world, father. For I have seen the working of the devil and his stench. His father too had known of this very thing, and said to him: If you had stayed forty days and kept my command to the end, you would have seen greater things.

fixed.before: Now there is war among those animals that occupy the same places and get their living from the same things. For if food is scarce, even animals of the same kind fight one another: they say, for instance, that the seals that live about the same place make war, male on male and female on female, until one kills the other or is driven out by it; and their young all do the same. Further, all animals are at war with the flesh-eaters, and these with the others, for their food comes from animals. This is why the seers take signs of 'sitting apart' and 'sitting together', counting as 'apart' the creatures that are hostile, and as 'together' those that are at peace with one another. It may well be that, if there were plenty of food, the animals that now fear men and are savage would be tame towards men, and towards one another in the same way. The care given to animals in Egypt makes this plain: because food is there and they are not in want, even the very wildest live together; for they are tamed by the benefits, as in some places the crocodile kind is tame towards the priest because he takes care to feed them. The same thing can be seen happening in other countries too, and in parts of them. The eagle and the snake are enemies, for the eagle feeds on snakes. So are the ichneumon and the venomous spider, for the ichneumon hunts these spiders. Among birds, the *poikilides*, the crested larks, the *pipra* and the *chloreus*, for they eat one another's eggs. And the crow and the owl: since the owl does not see sharply by day, the crow at midday snatches and eats its eggs, while the owl by night eats those of the crow; the one is the stronger by day, the other by night. The owl and the wren are also enemies, for the wren too eats the owl's eggs. By day the other small birds fly around the owl, which is called 'admiring' it, and fly at it and pluck its feathers; for this reason bird-catchers use it to catch all kinds of small birds. The bird called the 'old man' is also at war with the weasel and the crow, for they eat its eggs and its young. So are the turtle-dove and the *pyrallis*, for their feeding-ground and way of life are the same. And the green woodpecker and the *libyos*. And the kite and the raven: the kite takes from the raven whatever it has, because it is stronger in its claws and in flight, so that food makes these enemies too. Further, the birds that get their living from the sea are enemies to one another, such as the *brenthos*, the gull and the *harpē*. The buzzard is at war with the toad and the snake, for the buzzard eats them. The turtle-dove and the *chloreus*: the *chloreus* kills the turtle-dove, and the crow kills the bird called *typanos*. The *aigōlios* and the other birds with hooked talons eat the *kalaris*; hence the war between them. There is war too between the gecko and the spider, for the gecko eats spiders. And between the *pipo* and the heron, for it eats the heron's eggs and young. Between the *aigithos* and the ass there is war, because the ass, as it passes by, rubs its sores against the thorns; for this reason, and also if it brays, it throws out the eggs and the young, for they fall out in fright; and the bird, because of this harm, flies at it and pecks at its sores. The wolf is an enemy to the ass, the bull and the fox; for being a flesh-eater it attacks cattle, asses and the fox. So are the fox and the *kirkos*, for the same reason: being hook-taloned and a flesh-eater, it attacks and makes wounds with its blows. The raven too is an enemy to the bull and the ass, because it flies at them and strikes them and pecks their eyes. The eagle and the heron are also at war; for the eagle, being hook-taloned, attacks, and the heron dies defending itself. The *aisalōn* is an enemy to the vulture; and the *krex* to the *eleos*, the blackbird and the *chloriōn*, which some say in their tales was born from a funeral pyre; for it harms both them and their young. The nuthatch and the *trochilos* are enemies to the eagle; for the nuthatch breaks the eagle's eggs, and the eagle, both for this reason and because it is a flesh-eater, is an enemy to all. The *anthos* is an enemy to the horse, for the horse drives it out of the pasture; for the *anthos* feeds on grass, and it has a film over its eyes and is not sharp-sighted; it imitates the horse's voice, and frightens it by flying at it, and drives it out; but when [the horse] catches it, it kills it. The *anthos* lives by rivers and marshes; it has a fine colour and lives an easy life. The ass is an enemy to the *kōlōtēs* [lizard]; for [the lizard] sleeps in its manger and stops it eating by getting into its nostrils. Of herons there are three kinds: the *pellos*, the white, and the one called the *asterias* ('starry'). Of these the *pellos* couples and mates with difficulty; for it cries out and, as they say, sheds blood from its eyes when mating, and it lays its eggs badly and painfully. It is at war with those that harm it: the eagle (for it seizes it), the fox (for it destroys it at night) and the lark (for it steals its eggs). The snake is an enemy to the weasel and the pig: to the weasel when both are in a house, for they live on the same things; and the pig eats snakes. The *aisalōn* too is an enemy to the fox, for it strikes her and plucks her and kills her young; for it is hook-taloned. The raven and the fox are friends to each other, for the raven is at war with the *aisalōn*; and so it helps the fox when she is being struck. The vulture and the *aisalōn* are also enemies to each other, for both are hook-taloned. The vulture and the swan also fight the eagle, and the swan often wins; and of all birds, swans are the most given to killing one another. Among wild animals, some are always hostile to one another, others, as men are, when it so happens. The ass and the *akanthides* are enemies: they live off thistles, and the ass eats the thistles while they are tender. So are the *anthos*, the *akanthis* and the *aigithos*; and it is said that the blood of the *aigithos* and of the *anthos* will not mix together. The crow and the heron are friends, and the *schoiniōn* and the lark, and the *laedos* and the green woodpecker; for the green woodpecker lives by rivers and thickets, and the *laedos* among rocks and mountains, and it is attached to the place where it lives. And the *piphinx*, the *harpē* and the kite are friends; and the fox and the snake (for both live in holes); and the blackbird and the turtle-dove. The lion and the jackal are enemies to each other, for being flesh-eaters they live on the same things. Elephants too fight fiercely with one another and strike each other with their tusks; and the one that is beaten is utterly cowed, and cannot bear the voice of the victor. Elephants also differ from one another in courage to an astonishing degree. The Indians use the females for war as well as the males; the females, however, are smaller and much less spirited. The elephant knocks down walls by battering them with its great tusks, and palm trees with its forehead until it bends them over, and then, treading on them with its feet, it stretches them out on the ground. Elephants are hunted in this way: men mount some of the tame and brave ones and give chase, and when they catch up, they order these to strike them until they wear them out; then the elephant-driver leaps on and steers it with his sickle. Soon after this it is tamed and obeys. While the driver is mounted, all of them are gentle; but when he gets off, some are and some are not; and they bind the forelegs of those that turn savage with ropes, so that they keep quiet. They are hunted both when already full-grown and as young ones. So the friendships and wars of these animals come about because of their food and their way of life.

fixed.before: For those too who established these things are counted as condemned to the penalty of death: those angels, namely, who rushed down from heaven to the daughters of men, so that this disgrace also attaches to woman. For when they had betrayed to an age much more ignorant certain materials that had been well hidden and many arts that were not well revealed (for they had laid bare the workings of metals, and passed on the properties of herbs, and spread abroad the powers of incantations, and traced out every kind of curious inquiry even to the interpretation of the stars), they bestowed on women in particular, as if as their own special property, this equipment of womanly glory: the lustres of the little stones with which necklaces are made bright with colour, and the circlets of gold with which arms are clasped, and the dyes from orchil with which wool is coloured, and that very black powder with which the edges of the eyes are drawn out. What these things are like can for the present be declared already from the character and condition of their teachers: that sinners could neither show nor supply anything towards integrity, lovers nothing towards chastity, deserters of the spirit nothing towards the fear of God. If they are to be called teachings, bad masters must have taught badly; if wages for lust, the wage of nothing shameful is seemly. But what was so worth while in showing these things, as also in bestowing them? Could women not please men without the materials of splendour and without the devices of beauty, when, still unadorned and unarranged and, so to speak, raw and rough, they had moved angels? Or would the lovers have seemed mean and insulting, having had their use of them for nothing, if they had bestowed nothing on the women they had drawn into marriage? But this does not bear reckoning. The women who possessed angels could desire nothing more; they had made a great match, of course. Indeed [the angels], who no doubt at times thought from where they had fallen, and after the heated moments of their lusts sighed for heaven, repaid that very good of women, their natural beauty, as the cause of their evil, in such a way that their good fortune should not profit them, but that, drawn away from simplicity and sincerity, they should come, together with [the angels] themselves, into offence against God. They were sure that all glory and ambition and the desire of pleasing through the flesh is displeasing to God. These, surely, are the angels whom we are to judge; these are the angels whom we renounce in baptism; these certainly are the things through which they have deserved to be judged by man. What, then, are their things doing among their judges? What commerce is there between those who will condemn and those who are to be condemned? The same, I think, as between Christ and Belial. With what consistency do we mount that tribunal to give sentence against those whose gifts we covet? For to you too the same angelic substance is then promised, the same sex as to men; it promises you the same honour of judging. Unless, therefore, we already prejudge their things here, by condemning beforehand what we are going to condemn in them, they will rather judge and condemn us.

fixed.before: The ventriloquist says she has seen Samuel; she lies. Samuel was not brought up; Samuel does not speak. But just as there are some false prophets who say 'Thus says the Lord', and 'the Lord has not spoken', so this demon too lies, promising to bring up the one whom Saul orders. 'For whom shall I bring up?' she says. 'Bring up Samuel for me.' And these things are said by those who maintain that this [story] is not true: Samuel in Hades? Samuel brought up by a ventriloquist, the chosen one among the prophets, the one dedicated to God from his birth, the one of whom it was said in the temple before his birth that he would come to be, the one who as soon as he was weaned put on the ephod and the double cloak and became a priest of the Lord, to whom, while he was still a child, the Lord gave answer by speaking? Samuel in Hades? Samuel in the regions under the earth, he who succeeded Eli, who was condemned by providence for the sins and transgressions of his sons? Samuel in Hades, whom God heard at the time of the wheat harvest, and granted rain to come from heaven? Samuel in Hades, he who spoke out so boldly [to ask] whether he had taken anything that anyone prized? He did not take the calf, he did not take the ox; he judged the people and gave judgment on them while remaining poor; never did he desire to take anything from a people so great and so numerous. Samuel: why in Hades? Do you see what follows from 'Samuel in Hades'? Samuel in Hades? Why not Abraham too, and Isaac and Jacob, in Hades? Samuel in Hades? Why not Moses too, who is yoked together with Samuel according to the saying: 'Not even if Moses and Samuel should stand, not even them'? Samuel in Hades? Why not Jeremiah too in Hades, to whom it was said: 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came out of the womb I sanctified you'? In Hades Isaiah too, in Hades Jeremiah too, in Hades all the prophets, in Hades.
fixed.after: The ventriloquist says she has seen Samuel; she lies. Samuel was not brought up; Samuel does not speak. But just as there are some false prophets who say 'Thus says the Lord', when the Lord has not spoken, so this demon too lies, promising to bring up the one whom Saul orders. 'For whom shall I bring up?' she says. 'Bring up Samuel for me.' And these things are said by those who maintain that this [story] is not true: Samuel in Hades? Samuel brought up by a ventriloquist, the chosen one among the prophets, the one dedicated to God from his birth, the one of whom it was said in the temple before his birth that he would come to be, the one who as soon as he was weaned put on the ephod and the double cloak and became a priest of the Lord, to whom, while he was still a child, the Lord gave answer by speaking? Samuel in Hades? Samuel in the regions under the earth, he who succeeded Eli, who was condemned by providence for the sins and transgressions of his sons? Samuel in Hades, whom God heard at the time of the wheat harvest, and granted rain to come from heaven? Samuel in Hades, he who spoke out so boldly [to ask] whether he had taken anything that anyone prized? He did not take the calf, he did not take the ox; he judged the people and gave judgment on them while remaining poor; never did he desire to take anything from a people so great and so numerous. Samuel: why in Hades? Do you see what follows from 'Samuel in Hades'? Samuel in Hades? Why not Abraham too, and Isaac and Jacob, in Hades? Samuel in Hades? Why not Moses too, who is yoked together with Samuel according to the saying: 'Not even if Moses and Samuel should stand, not even them'? Samuel in Hades? Why not Jeremiah too in Hades, to whom it was said: 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came out of the womb I sanctified you'? In Hades Isaiah too, in Hades Jeremiah too, in Hades all the prophets, in Hades.

fixed.before: Often I have been urged to set out on the present undertaking, and have held back, 'yielding neither to sloth nor to thoughtlessness of mind', as the poet says, but above all awed by the grandeur and the number of the principles it contains, and fearing the objections of men who say what they say either because they are convinced that there is no divination and no providence of the gods, or else because they are providing themselves with exercises and pastimes. But now the present need, pressing because of its usefulness not only to ourselves but also to the men who will come after us, has urged me not to delay or put it off, but to write down whatever I have an understanding of, an understanding I acquired through experience. And I think that I shall gain two things from such a work: that I shall stand against those who try to do away with divination itself and its kinds, both without giving offence and with no ordinary argument, bringing into the open my experience and the testimony of the outcomes, which would be enough to withstand all men; and further, that for those who make use of divination but, because they have not met with accurate accounts of these matters, have gone astray and are now in danger of despising it and falling away from it, I shall establish a saving cure in place of their error. For nearly all those a little older than ourselves, wishing to win a reputation as writers, and thinking that they would become famous by this alone, if they left behind treatises on the interpretation of dreams, have made copies of one another, either explaining badly what was well said by the ancients, or adding many untrue things to a few of the ancients'; for they wrote not from experience but improvising, each as he was moved about any given thing; and some had read all the books of the ancients, others not all, for some, being rare through their age and corrupted, escaped their notice. But I, for my part, on the one hand, there is no book of dream interpretation that I have not acquired, since I have great zeal for this; on the other hand, though the diviners in the marketplace are greatly slandered, whom those who put on solemn faces and raise their eyebrows call beggars and sorcerers and buffoons, I despised the slander and for many years kept company with them, both in Greece, in its cities and at its festivals, and in Asia and in Italy and in the largest and most populous of the islands, patiently listening to old dreams and their outcomes; for there was no other way to get practice in these matters. From this it has come about that I have, in abundance, more to say about each thing than one might expect, and so as, speaking the very truth, not to talk idly; and, for whatever I mention, to give proofs that are clear and easily grasped by all, and from simple [principles], unless something should be so plain that I consider an explanation of it superfluous.

not_upheld.f4#3: Vitae Patrum: 'quadringinta panes' read as forty loaves (a late spelling of quadraginta), matching the forty days of the same sentence; a note explains.
not_upheld.f4#4: Orphic fragment (Damascius): 'Necessity, who is of the same nature, and Adrasteia' is the usual construal (so Kirk, Raven and Schofield); Ananke and Adrasteia are named together.
